title: Repeated lawsuit numbers, waivers and settlement payments
question: Which repeated amounts are real obligations, revised agreements, internal transfers or payments to another public body?
finding: Six comparisons against signed records show how lawsuit totals can overstate payments, omit noncash terms or send a recovery to the wrong government.
how: Screened 16,882 San Francisco legislative matters dated January 2, 2014 through November 17, 2026. Docket patterns identified 714 matters and 693 distinct case numbers. Of those case numbers, 33 appeared on multiple matters with monetary terms. A separate text search found 54 conditional settlement matters and 130 waiver or receipt intersections. The groups overlap.
limits: The docket patterns miss case numbers omitted from titles and nonstandard identifiers. These six comparisons do not establish the outcome of all 33 groups. Authorizations and signed terms establish receipts only where a separate record confirms payment.

rows.test: Does a closing order give the entire settlement?
rows.record: Forty-six orders in the Mission flood litigation total $14,413,156.25. Twelve orders match $4,946,480 paid in December 2021. The later $865,000 reserve movement reimbursed the utility.
rows.limit: Obtain the remaining payment schedule and the allocation of interest and legal costs.

source.t: January 2022 legislative analysis, twelve settlements paid in December and reserve reimbursement

comparison.t: January 2022 committee transmission to Controller of authorized internal fund release

rows.test: Does a revised fee settlement count twice?
rows.record: The revised sign-permit litigation agreement expressly modified the old $500,000 terms to $580,000. The confirmed $250,000 escrow and 12 installments of $27,500 reconcile to $580,000.
rows.limit: The revised ordinance establishes the payment schedule. Request the final disbursements.

source.t: Ordinance 258-19, original attorney fee claim and escrow

comparison.t: Ordinance 180-21, revised fee claim and 12 installments

rows.test: Did the City owe both payments with the same face value?
rows.record: A vehicle accident damaged City and adjacent property. The Board approved $273,853.76 on the insurer’s claim against the City and the same amount payable to the City on a cross-complaint against 691 O’Farrell, LLC. A co-defendant had a separate $500,000 obligation.
rows.limit: The offsetting authorized amounts do not prove settlement dates, final cost or the posting method.

comparison.t: City’s cross-complaint against a property owner

rows.test: Can separate utility lawsuits filed the same day be joined by payer alone?
rows.record: Ordinance 079-15 pairs $1,563,963.29 owed in each direction across a Ferry Building power case and a franchise-fee case. Separate Ordinance 176-15 authorizes $1,594,700 on a neighboring case number.
rows.limit: Request the executed settlements and Controller postings for each case.

source.t: Ordinance 079-15, Ferry Building service and matching franchise payment obligations

comparison.t: Ordinance 176-15, separate case with limited release of claims

rows.test: Are settlements in the same courthouse all City recoveries?
rows.record: Three municipal bond-insurance orders authorize $1,247,793 for San Francisco. Oakland separately authorized $25,830.33 in a different case in the same court county against one of the same insurers.
rows.limit: The independent Oakland resolution resolves a contradictory payer in a staff memo. Neither figure is proof of actual receipts.

comparison.t: Adopted Oakland Resolution 84850, different docket and settling insurer

rows.test: Can a $0 settlement materially change a rule?
rows.record: The airline settlement conditions dismissal on a change to worker health coverage and allows the trade group to reopen the case if new legislation increases employer obligations. The City enacted the companion rule.
rows.limit: Employer participation, worker costs and the final court entry remain separate questions.

source.t: Ordinance 212-26, settlement condition and reinstatement terms

comparison.t: Ordinance 213-26, new minimum expenditure formula and weekly cap
